rows.Title: Differences in Race Characteristics between World-Class Individual-Medley and Stroke-Specialist Swimmers
rows.Aims: - To investigate differences between world-class IM and stroke-specialists by comparing each lap of 200 m IM and the corresponding lap in 200 m stroke events
rows.Hypothesis: there would be no effects of sex and stroke on the difference between IM and stroke events
rows.Population: - 80 races (40 male: 24.2yrs \pm 3.6 and WA points: 906 \pm 37; 40 female: age: 23.9yrs \pm 4.4 and WA points: 880 \pm 39)
rows.Event:
- 200m IM, FL, BA, BR, FR
- LC
rows.Data Collection: - Video from 2021 European Champs
rows.Methods:
- Race videos were analyzed (to GB standard)

- to compare IM swimmers and stroke-specialists, data were taken from laps 1-4 from the 200m FL, BA, BR, and FR

IM swimmers Vs Stroke-specialists
- absolute parameter values (SR and other race parameters) were compared between groups via independent sample t-test
- Pairs' effect size was calculate with Cohen's d or r-value (if non-parametric test was used)

Effect of Sex
- 2-way ANOVA (sex X Stroke) was used to determine differences between groups (specialists vs IM swimmers)
- partial eta-squared was calculated
- post-hoc comparisons were performed with Holm-Sidak correction
rows.Independent Variable(s):
- Stroke
- Group (IM swimmer or stroke-specialist)
- Sex
rows.Results:
- BR specialists showed a faster clean-swimming speed for males and  females) than IM swimmers
- In males, clean swimming speed in FR specialists was about 2% faster than IM swimmers
- In females, IM swimmers showed a 4% higher FL clean swimming speed than FL specialists
- In male and female BR-specialists, DPS was about 17% longer than IM swimmers while SR did not differ
- Male & female stroke specialists showed 14-37% faster underwater speed in BA and FR than IM swimmers
- No differences between groups for breakout distance and time (except for mens FR-specialists and IM swimmers)
-  Male FL specialists showed 6% longer underwater time than male IM swimmers
- female BR specialists showed a 5% slower underwater speed compared to IM swimmers

2-Way ANOVA
- Significant interaction between Sex X Stroke (clean swimming speed & underwater speed)
- sign. stroke effects were observed for all other variables (except underwater distance)

Post-Hoc comparisons
- Relative FL clean swimming speed was 5% higher in females than males for IM swimmers, as was underwater speed during BR
- Relative clean swimming FL speed was sign. higher than other stroke in females
- In Males, relative BR clean swimming speed was slower compared to FL and BA, and FR was lower than BA
- Relative breakout time was longer for FR than the other 3 strokes
- Relative SR in BR was higher than FL and FR
- BR showed longer relative DPS than FL, BA and FR
- Relative DPS in BA was shorter compared to FL
rows.Conclusion:
- IM swimmers show similar performance in FL, BA, and FR to stroke-specialists in 200 m races
- BR specialists’ performance in 200 m races (lap 3) is better than that of IM swimmers, due to a longer DPS
- IM swimmers have the potential to improve more in BR than in the other three strokes
- Males and females generally showed a similar trend in the difference between IM swimmers and specialists, except for faster clean-swimming speed in lap 1 (FL) in female IM swimmers compared to FL specialists
rows.Notes: - used partial-eta-squared instead of eta-squared for 2-way ANOVA
rows.Extra:
Stroke: SR (15-35), DPS
Velocity: FSS (break-45)
Underwater: wall-break (s,v)

1. Shapiro-Wilk
2. Independent T-test or Mann-Whitney U
3. post-hoc w/ Holm-sidak correction
4. Cohen's d or r-value

2. 2-way ANOVA
3. Partial eta-squared
4. Box-Cox transformation (for non-normal data)
5. post-hoc w/ Holm-sidak correction

- how does r-value and MWU test work together? (effect size for MWU is rank-biserial correlation which is shown as r and is interpreted the same)
- used MWU to compare performance metric differences between stroke specialists and IM swimmers

rows.Title: Variation in competition performance,  number of races, and age: Long-term athlete  development in elite female swimmers
rows.Aims: 1. To analyze potential success factors for international swimming competitions, i.e., annual variation in competition performance (AVCP), number of races per year, and age, with particular focus on female swimmers throughout the 10-years prior to the 2018EC
rows.Hypothesis:
1. Athletes ranked higher at the 2018EC will show higher consistency in performance with lower AVCP
2. Athletes ranked higher at the 2018EC will compete in a greater number of races per year, and (3) are older than their lower ranked counterparts
rows.Population:
- Females finalists (n=253)
- Total of 40,277 races over 10 years
rows.Data Collection:
- Data from SwimRankings DB
- Data of the 2018 European Champs finalists were retrospectively collected (10yrs)
rows.Methods:
- CV was calculated with the STDEV divided by the mean swimming times in that particular year and event to derive AVCP (Annual Variation in Competition Performance) for each event
- Outliers were removed

Statistical Analysis
- AVCP, number of races per year, and age were correlated with the 2018EC ranking for all ten years preceding the championships (2018–2009) using Pearson’s correlation coefficient
- 2-way ANOVA was used to compare all 10 yrs prior to 2018 EC (authors don't state the variables used but it looks like number of races -> Stroke X Distance)
- Multiple linear regression was used to determine the relationship between AVCP/number of races per year/Age and ranking
- Effect size (Cohen's f^2) was calculated for the regression model
rows.Dependent Variable(s):
- Ranking (in 2018 European Champs) (regression)
- AVCP (descriptive)
- Number of races per year (descriptive)
- Age (descriptive)
rows.Independent Variable(s):
- AVCP (regression)
- Number of races per year (regression)
- Age (regression)
- Year
rows.Results:
Pearson Correlations
- AVCP decreased over the 10yr for all strokes, and was lowest for FR but not different between FL, BA, BR, and IM
- No relationship between AVCP and 2018EC ranking

ANOVA
- Number of races per year increased across the 10yrs in all strokes but IM
- Sig. interaction effect showed an incresing number of races for 50, 100, and 200m races
- Across all strokes and distances, swimmers who ranked higher (at 2018EC) participated in sig. more races for all 10yrs prior to the 2018EC

Correlational Analysis
- small-medium effects for most of hte 10yrs for FL, BR, and FR
- effects were less clear but evident for BA and IM
- for race distance, higher ranking correlated with sig. more races for most of the 10yrs (med-large effects for 50, 100, and 200m; association between ranking and race participation was unclear for 400, 800, and 1500m)
- Older athletes were generally more successful across all strokes and distances

Regression Analysis
- R^2 = 0.22 with medium effect size for pooled data of all strokes and race distances
- 2018EC ranking remained unaffected by AVCP
- Highly significant effect for age and number of races -> higher ranked swimmers were older and participated more often per year
- For race distance, model explained sig. portion of the rankings with large effect sizes (50m: 0.43, 100m: 0.34, 200m: 0.35, 400m: 0.49) with number of races per year and age having a sig. effect 
- 800 and 1500m remained unexplained 
- No race distances were affected by AVCP
rows.Conclusion:
- 2018EC ranking was unaffected by AVCP for all races swum throughout the year
- Higher ranked swimmers competed in more races per year
- Older swimmers were generally more successful across all stokes and distances
rows.Notes: - Some of the sentences in this article are a little funny to me
rows.Stats Flow:
1. Histogram and QQ plot
2. Pearson's correlation

2. 2-way ANOVA 
3. Bonferroni post-hoc

2. Multiple linear regression
3. Cohen's f^2
rows.Stats Comments:
- Subjective normality testing
- No equality of variance test

rows.Title: Are the 50m Race Segments Changed From Heats to Finals at the 2021 European Swimming Championships?
rows.Aims:
1. study the coefficient of variation (CV) and performance progress (%Δ) in total time (i.e., T50) in the four different swimming strokes
2. specifically analyze which of the race segments and stroke variables are most modified to achieve improvement across the rounds
rows.Hypothesis:
1. performance would improve over the rounds
2. changes would be a consequence of the improvement in the performance variables corresponding to the different segments of the race
rows.Population:
- 322 performances (56 males and 60 females)
- Races from finalist athletes in heats, semi-finals, and finals
rows.Data Collection:
- Official times from LEN
- Video from 2021 European Champs
rows.Methods:
- Race videos were analyzed (to GB standard)

- Linear mixed effects models were applied between rounds (e.g., heats, semifinals, and final), for all swimmers and performance variables to estimate means (fixed effects) and within-swimmer variations
- fixed main effects were event (50 m freestyle, breaststroke, backstroke and butterfly), performance variables (i.e., the ones presented in Table 1) and rounds

- Performance variables between rounds were compared with repeated-measures ANOVA -> verified by Bonferroni post-hoc
- Effect sizes were calculated (Eta-squared)

- Pearson correlations between all variables and times at 15, 25, and 50m were obtained
- Simple linear regression was then used to evaluate the relationships
rows.Independent Variable(s):
- Event
- Performance Variables
- Round (heat, semi-finals, finals)
- inter-lap distance (T15, T25, and T50)
rows.Results:
Linear Mixed Effects models
- Sign. progression of performance was observed in most of the events over the rounds
- The largest CV was noted in FL events, followed by FR, BA, and BR
- it is unclear which variable (distance or time) had a larger partial contribution to underwater speed

Correlational Analysis
- In most events the correlation between T15 and T25, and between T25 and T50 was very large
- Correlation between T15 and T50 was moderate or large for the finalists
- SR15-25 m and SR35-45 m increased over the competitions
- SL was prone to decrease most of the times, trading off with the faster SR

Regression Analysis
- Supplementary material
rows.Conclusion:
- Intra-individual performances varied in a significant range of 0.5–0.7%
- There were significant  improvements in T50 as the competition progressed (except men's BR)
- It was a common tendency to reduce the underwater phase and increase SR with the aim of increasing speed
rows.Limitations: - Results from elite population may not translate to slower populations
rows.Notes: - Used eta-squared for RM ANOVA and not partial eta-squared

rows.Title: Start Fast, Swim Faster, Turn Fastest: Section Analyses and Normative Data for Individual Medley
rows.Aims:
1. To provide benchmarks and normative data for fastest and slowest European Championship participants in 100 m, 200 m, and 400 m short-course IM races
2. Investigate differences between the various swimming strokes and turns involved in IM
3. To quantify the effect and contribution of various race sections on swimming performance
rows.Population:
- 320 IM Races (8 finalists and 8 slowest males and females)
- Males: WA points = 806 \pm 75
- Females: WA points = 772 \pm 75
rows.Data Collection: - Video from 2019 European Short Course Champs
rows.Methods:
- Race videos were analyzed (to GB standard)

- Start and race times were compared between finalists and the 8 slowest (same event) using an unpaired t-test
- Turn and swim parameters were compared using 3 separate 2-way ANOVAs: 1. (Group X Stroke) or (Group X type of Turn) or (Group X Race section)
- Effect size was calculated (partial eta-squared)

- Stepwise regression was used to determine the effects of race section on performance with start time, turn time, swim velocity, SR, and DPS as predictors

- Pearson’s product-moment correlation coefficient was used to relate start, turn, swim, and stroke parameters to race time with coefficients
rows.Dependent Variable(s):
- Start time (t-test)
- Turn time (t-test)
- Race time
rows.Independent Variable(s):
- Group (finalists or bottom 8)
- Stroke
- Type of turn
- Race section
- Start time
- Turn time
- Swim Velocity
- SR
- DPS
rows.Results:
Starts and Turns
- ANOVA showed sign. main effects for all events
- Female finalists had sign. faster turn times in all turn types and race distances
- Male finalists had sign. faster turn times in all events except for FL to BA in 400m IM
- FL/BA turn was faster compared to BA/BR and BR/FR turns
- Male finalists showed faster swim velocities compared to bottom8 swimmers, except for BR during 100m and FL/BA during the 400m
- female finalists were faster than bottom8 except FL/BR for 100m 
- FL and FR showed faster swim velocities followed by BA and BA
- SR and DPS did not differ between finalist and bottom8 (males and females)
- FL showed the highest SR with no differences between BA, BR, and FR
- DPS was not different between strokes of females finalists
- Bottom8 female 100m swimmers showed lower DPS for FL and BR compared to BA and FR

Parameter Contribution
- Finalists were sign. faster (total time) in all race distances
- % contribution had similar trends in both groups (highest for Turn and lower for Start)
- Turn contribution increased from 100m to 400m while start section contribution decreased

Stepwise Regression
- explained 97-100% of the dependant variable
- Turn time had the largest effect on race time, followed by swim velocity (all distances and both males & females)
- Start time effected only 100 and 200m events
- SR & DPS had no effect on the regression model

Correlation analysis
- Very large correlations between start performance and 100 & 200m race times in both sexes
- 400m IM: start performance was only correlated with race time in females
- Turn time and swim velocity showed very large correlations (r >0.7)
- SR showed no correlations 
- DPS showed medium correlations with race time in male swimmers
rows.Conclusion:
- Start and turn times were shown to be strong predictors of performance 
- Segment contribution did not appear to differ between finalists and bottom8
- BR may provide the largest potential for future development in IM race times
- DPS, rather than SR, was shown as a performance indicator for stroke mechanics
rows.Notes: - I feel like the segment contribution methods could be refined to better differentiate sub-groups

Velocity: 15-20, 10-20
Turn: total

2. QQ plot
3.  t-test
4. 2-way ANOVA

rows.Title: Performance Development of European Swimmers Across the Olympic Cycle
rows.Aims:
1. To quantify the performance development of race times and key performance indicators in European swimmers across the last Olympic cycle (from 2016 to 2021)
2. To provide reference values for long-course pool  events of top elite swimmers for both sexes from 50 m to 1,500 m including BU, BA, BR, FR, and IM
rows.Population: - 246 men (WA points: 890 \pm 40) and 256 women (WA points: 879 \pm 38)
rows.Data Collection:
- Data from SwimRankings
- Olympic Games & European Champs
rows.Methods:
- Race videos were analyzed (to GB standard)
- analyses were conducted on data grouped by event and gender

- Descriptive stats were calculated
- Race time development at the Olympic games and European Championships across the 5-year Olympic cycle was determined with a 2-way ANOVA (competition X Year)

- Reference values were established based on the mean values of the finalists in the 2021 European Champs

- Differences between the 2016 and 2021 European Champs were assessed via t-test
- Cohen's d effect sizes were calculated
rows.Dependent Variable(s):
- Race time
- Race metrics (for reference values)
rows.Independent Variable(s):
- Year
- Competition
rows.Results:
- Race times sig. improved from 2016 to 2021 in 6 events for males (100 BA/BR/FR and 200 BR/FR/IM) and 2 events for females (100 BR and 50 FR)
- European men's race times approximated the Olympic level
- 10 mens events in 2016 were sign. faster at the Olympic games than European Champs (only 2 for 2021 comparison)
- 9 and 7 womens events were sign. faster at the Olympic games than in the 2016 and 2021 European Champs

5-year cycle changes
- Start times improved (15 events for men, 14 for women)
- Turn-times remained inconclusive (men & women)
- Generally, breakout distances increased
- Clean swimming velocities became faster (12 events for men, 5 for women)
- Effect size indicated an inverse relationship between reduced stroke rate and increased distance per stroke (particular for BA and FR)
rows.Conclusion:
- Male European swimmers approximated performance levels at the Olympic games and showed improved race times from 2016 to 2021
- Female European swimmers sign. improved in only 2 events across the 5-year timespan and remained slower in 7 events compared to Olympic finalists
- Start performances, longer breakouts, and improved clean swimming speeds were shown to be key performance indicators
- Effect sizes indicated reduced stroke rate in alternating swimming strokes
rows.Notes:
- This is probably the only article to analyze any changes in race parameters over time, however, it didnt really determine the relationships between the parameters and performance
- Stats methods section is messy and not super clear

rows.Title: Contributions of each of the four swimming strokes to elite 200-400 individual medley swimming performance in short and long course competitions
rows.Aims: to assess the strokes that have more influence on the performance in the 200 and 400 m IM swimming performances of elite male and female swimmers
rows.Population:
- 1095 swimmers (male and female)
- Minimum of 800 WA points
rows.Data Collection:
- Data from WA DB
- Competitions included World Champs (LC & SC) and Olympics (LC)
rows.Methods:
- Splits were converted to Z-score
- data were organized by gender, event, and pool length

- Linear regression was used to determine the relationship between Z-scores and FINA points

- A Decision tree was used to determine the relationship between swimming style (Z-scores -> pacing) and final position (medallist 1-3, finalist 4-8, and rest)
- 4 trees were derived: (1) long-course, (2) short-course, (3) Olympic Games, and (4) World Championships
- used a 70:30 train-test split
rows.Independent Variable(s):
- Gender
- Distance
- Pool type (25m or 50m)
- Split (stroke) -> 0-100 for 400m IM
- Performance group (medallist, finalist, or rest)
rows.Results:
FINA points & Z-scores
- All 5 models showed high R^2 values (~0.9)
- Most influential strokes were BA & BR, followed by FL and FR
- FR was more influential in SC than in LC, while BR was more influential in LC than SC
- FL was less influential in women than men

Performance Group Classification
-  73% accurate in SC; medal position is essentially due to a BR Z-score <-67%, and BA Z-score <-52%
- 82% accurate in LC; medal position is related to: FL Z-score <-68%, BR Z-score < -55%, and BA Z-score < -31%
- 75% accurate for Olympic games; (Authors did not mention the Z-score details for this tree model)
- 79% accurate for World Champs: due to: BR Z-score < -54% and BA Z-score < -98%
rows.Conclusion:
- The most influential strokes within the IM are BA on FINA points
- In SC swimming, the most influential stroke was BA
- In LC swimming, the most influential stroke was BA and BR
- By gender, males and females were influenced the most by BA and BR
- FINA points and Z-scores have a strong relationship
rows.Notes: - I am surprized that the authors did not mention pacing all too much within their title

rows.Author(s): Catarina C. Santos, Ricardo J. Fernandes, Daniel A. Marinho, and Mário J. Costa
rows.Keywords: Swimming, swimmers, analysis, race, competition
rows.Title: From Entry to Finals: Progression and Variability of Swimming Performance at the 2022 FINA World Championships
rows.Aims:
1. Analyze the progression of men’s and women’s (FINA A and B qualifying standards) swimming (race time), performance improvement (%IMP), and variability (%CV) between entry times and the best performances in the 50, 100, and 200 m for all competitive swimming techniques
2. Analyze specifically the entry times and all rounds, i.e., entry-heats, heats-semifinals, and semifinals-finals in men and women Top16, semifinalists, and finalists
rows.Hypothesis: - The best performances achieved in all rounds would be below the entry times (evidencing a negative %IMP) and the finalists would demonstrate a higher and positive %IMP (mainly between heats and semifinals) than their remaining counterparts
rows.Population: - 1102 individual performances (629 men, 473 women)
rows.Event:
- 50, 100, and 200m FR, BA, BR, and FL
- LC
rows.Data Collection:
- Data from OmegaTiming and WA db
- Data was retrospectively collected from qualifiers of 2022 World Champs (LC)
rows.Methods:
- Top16 (semi-finalists and finalists) were extracted for each event

- Shapiro-Wilk and Levene tests for normality and homoscedasticity 
- Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used to compare entry times and best performances (if violations were determined)
	- Effect size was calculated (didn't say F or d)

- Repeated measures ANOVA (with bonferroni post-hoc) was used to analyze the variation between rounds of the Top16 in the entry-heats, and finals/semi-finals pairs
	- Partial eta-squared was used to determine effect size
- % performance change between rounds was calculated
- The variation of the swimmers' performance between rounds was computed and transformed into %
rows.Dependent Variable(s):
- Entry Times
- Best Performances
- Swim Time
- % change between heats & semi-finals/finals
rows.Independent Variable(s): - Heat type (entry-heats or semi-finals/finals)
rows.Results:
- Differences between entry times and best performances were found with moderate to large effect in all events, except 200FR in females and 50BA/50FL in both
- Men showed the greatest performance decrease in 200m BA & BR, and the lowest in 100FR and 50BA
- Women showed the greatest performance decrease in 100/200 BA/BR, and the lowest in 50BA and 20 FR/FL
- intra-swimmer CV ranged between 0.75-1.14% in men and between 0.69-1.16% in women

- Round effect differences were found in most events with moderate to large effect sizes, except 50 BR/FL for all groups, 100 FR/BR and 200FL for semi-finalists, and 50BA for finalists

MEN
- round-to-round analysis showed that most of the entry-heats performances decreased for the top16, and the heat-semifinals round increases were mainly found for the finalists group
- All 50m performances remained unchanged between heats and semi-finals/finals
- %CV tended to be lower in semi-finalists than finalists

WOMEN
- most events showing differences with minimum to strong effect for all swimmer groups
- No diff in 50BR for all groups, and no diff in 50 BA/FL, 100 FR/FL, and 200FR for semi-finalists

rows.Title: Pacing Behavior Development in Adolescent Swimmers: A Large-Scale Longitudinal Data Analysis
rows.Aims: 1. To investigate the development of pacing behaviour in adolescent swimmers, specifically disentangling the effects of age and experience and differentiating between performance levels in adulthood
rows.Hypothesis:
1. The pacing behaviour of swimmers would develop during adolescence, gradually exhibiting more resemblance to adult behaviour
2. Independent of age, increased experience would facilitate a better fit with the task demands: a higher velocity in the initial stages in the shorter tasks and an overall more even distribution of effort in longer tasks
3. Adolescent swimmers who reached a higher performance level in adulthood will exhibit a pacing behaviour more resembling that of an adult swimmer
4. The split between swimmers of different future performance levels would occur earlier in female compared with male swimmers
rows.Population:
Initial Sample:
- 100-m freestyle: 2,773,387 observations
- 200-m freestyle: 1,842,992

Final Sample:
100m: 
- 1,839 males 8,576 races
- 1,659 female 7,384 races

200m:
- 978 males  4,897 races
- 1,252 females 5,412 races

- Performance classes were determined by relative Seasonal Best time (rSBT)
rows.Data Collection:
- SwimRankings DB
- Competitions are unknown (likely not included due to data being so large)
rows.Methods:
Data Processing:
- performances over 180 s (100-m freestyle) and 360 s (200-m freestyle) were excluded
- Data from 2008-10 were removed
- Data from season 2019–2020 were excluded (due to impacted training opportunities)
- Season best time (SBT) and age at SBT was calculated for each swimmer
- only swimmers who had at least one swim performance in the age category of 22 yr or older (male) or 20 yr or older (female) were included
- performances after the swimmer’s career-best swim performance were excluded
- Relative section times (RST) were calculated (% in each split-section)
- Relative (rSBT) was calculated based on SBT and the years WR
- Swimmers were organized into 3 groups (elite, sub-elite, or high-competitive) by their all-time rSBT after peak performance age

Statistics
- longitudinal multilevel models were created to describe pacing behaviour as a function of age, race experience (both log transformed), and performance group
- Post hoc analyses were performed for models with future performance group as a significant predictor variable
	• Swimmers were classified based on age category, then an independent t-test was conducted to examine from which the age onward between-group differences in pacing behaviour occurred
rows.Independent Variable(s):
- Age
- Race experience
- Performance group
rows.Results:
AGE:
- Older male swimmers were relatively faster in the 1st 50m of the 100m
- No effect in females in the 100m
- 200m: older males and females were predicted to start relatively slower, have a relatively faster middle section, and have a relatively slower final 50m section

RACE EXPERIENCE:
- Sig impacted RST in all segments (except final segment in male 200m)
- 100m: more experienced males and females were relatively slower in the first half of the race
- 200m: males with more race experience were relatively slower in the 1st 50m but faster in the 150m section; more experienced females were relatively slower in the 1st 50m section and relatively faster in the 150 & 200m sections

PERFORMANCE LEVEL:
- 100m:
	• Elite males were faster in the 1st 50m when compared to high-competitive 
	• Post hoc analysis showed elite males differentiating themselves at 17yo
	• No difference in females of differing performance groups
- 200m:
	• Elite males were predicted to be relatively slower in the 1st 50m but faster in the 150m section (compared to high-competitive)
	• Male elite group differentiated themselves as early as 16
	• Elite females were relatively slower in the 1st 50m but faster in the 150 & 200m sections (compared to high-competitive)
	• Female elite group differentiated themselves as early as 13
- In both events, the model predicted no significant difference in RST between the elite and sub-elite groups
rows.Conclusion:
- In males, the effect of age and performance group was also more pronounced in the 200-m event compared with the 100-m event
- Elite 100m males were faster in the 1st 50m
- Elite 200m males and females were slower in the 1st 50m but faster in the final sections
rows.Limitations: - models do not account for all the variance in a swimmers’ pacing behaviour
rows.Notes: - This paper serves as a good stepping stone for some improvements to be made for a new study on pacing analysis

rows.Title: Differences between elite and sub-elite swimmers in a 100 m breaststroke: a new race analysis approach with time-series velocity data
rows.Aims: 1. To investigate differences throughout 100 m breaststroke between elite and sub-elite swimmers using time-series velocity data
rows.Hypothesis: 1. Elite swimmers would show a higher velocity than sub-elite swimmers during the surface swimming and the pull-out phases, in which they perform propulsive limb motions
rows.Population: - 14 males BR specialists (7 elite: finalists at SC nationals in 100m BR; 7 Sub-elite: qualified for  national champs) (Norway) (WA points > 700)
rows.Data Collection:
- Data were recorded and analyzed via AIM race analysis system (10 camera system: 5 above- and 5 below-water)
- Race data from training (max effort bouts)
rows.Methods:
- Collected data from the analysis and timing systems
	• Flight time/distance, pivot time (turn time), velocity (m/s)
	• Each lap was divided into 3 segments: glide, pull-out, and clean swimming
- Velocity data was then smoothed via Butterworth low-pass

- Basic profile info and all variables for the 1st lap were analysed using an independent-samples t-test
- Variables for laps 2-4 were assessed via 2-way ANOVA (Lap X Group)
	• For variables with significant main effects, multiple comparisons were conducted with a paired or independent sample t-test with the Holm–Bonferroni method for the alpha level adjustment
- Data normality checked via Shapiro-Wilks
	• Non-normal variables were transformed using Box-Cox transformation
- For the time-series velocity data in each segment, a statistical parametric mapping (SPM) constituted by t-statistics was employed for between-groups comparison
rows.Dependent Variable(s):
- Velocity
- Basic profile info (height, weight, age)
rows.Independent Variable(s):
- Performance group
- Lap
rows.Results:
- No significant differences in age or height between the groups, but there was a 7kg weight difference in elite than sub-elite swimmers
- Elite swimmers complete the time-trial faster
- elite swimmers achieved a longer flight distance despite the similar flight time
- No differences were observed in the glide and pull-out in the 1st lap
	• But the elite swimmers swam a shorter clean-swimming distance with a higher mean clean-swimming velocity
- Laps 2-4:
	• main effect of group was observed in the clean-swimming duration, distance, and mean velocity as well as the mean glide velocity
	• In the clean-swimming segment, multiple comparisons detected differences between the groups in the mean velocity and duration on all three laps, but not in the distance travelled
	• elite swimmers showed higher glide velocity than the sub-elite swimmers during the 2nd and 3rd lap but not the 4th
	
- In all laps, elite swimmers had a higher velocity during a large part of the free swimming segment
	• But not at the beginning of the segment
- In the 1st lap, glide velocity was faster in the elite group from approximately the 20th to the 40th percentile of the segment time, while from the 2nd to 4th lap, the difference was observed at the beginning of the segment
- No difference was observed in the pull-out velocity at any point
rows.Conclusion:
- No differences in the pull out segment between the groups
- elite swimmers generally showed a faster mean glide velocity after the turns (non-significant)
- ANOVA did not provide any interaction between the factors
- Elite-swimmers were significantly faster in the clean-swimming duration, distance, and mean velocity
	• Also faster mean glide velocity
rows.Limitations:
- Data were taken from trials, potentially eliminating any effects from competition
- Small sample size -> inflated type 2 error
rows.Notes: - SPM seems like an interesting method but I'm not totally sure about how it works (from what I do understand, it uses GLMS at some point)
rows.Future Research: - what differentiates the glide performance between elite and sub-elite swimmers?

- The dataset with the highest accuracy was selected to run explanations and visualizations

applied Bayesian change point detection method to identify specific points where shifts in values within the PDP occurred

- Highest importance score was “velocity in the 65- to 70-m race segment” (0.086)

rows.Title: Effect of Age, Sex, and Race Distance on Front Crawl Stroke Parameters in Subelite Adolescent Swimmers  During Competition
rows.Aims:
1. to determine the main effect of age, sex and race distance on four stroke parameters (v, SR, SL, SI) and examine the confounding effects of these independent variables
2. to investigate the pacing strategies of these swimmers by quantifying changes in stroke parameters between race quarters of the 100 m and 200 m events
rows.Hypothesis:
1. stroke parameters would be influenced by age, sex and race distance
2. The stroke parameters would change between race quarters
rows.Population:
- 112 adolescent swimmers (56 females, 56 males)
- 2 age groups: 12-14 and 15-18
- 2 performance groups: Elite and sub-elite (athletes who have yet to represent their country internationally)
rows.Data Collection:
- Video from International Schools Championships
- Race times were taken from official results
rows.Methods:
Data Organization
- Speed was calculated between 15-20m for the 1st length and middle 10m for the remaining
- SR was calculated determined by the time to complete 3 stroke cycles
- Stroke length (SL) was calculated by dividing velocity by SR
- SI (Stroke index) was calculated from the SL and velocity

Statistical Analysis
- Normality tested via Shapiro-Wilk test
	• SI was log-transformed due to normality violations
- Descriptive statistics were calculated for each metric
- MONOVA was used to examine the effect of Age, Sex, and Race distance on each of the stroke metrics
- Homogeneity of variance was determined using Levene's test
	• Box test showed a violation
	• Pilliai's stat was set to 0.01 to ensure robustness
- Friedman's repeated-measures ANOVA was used to determine the changes in stroke metrics across race quarters (determining pacing relationships of stroke metrics)
- Post hoc Wilcoxon matched-pair tests were then applied alongside Bonferroni corrections
rows.Dependent Variable(s):
- Velocity
- Stroke Rate
- Stroke Length
- Stroke Index
rows.Independent Variable(s):
- Age
- Sex
- Race distance
- Race quarter
rows.Results:
- Velocity, SL, and SI significantly differed between age groups, sexes and race distances
	• Main reason was that the males in the older group swam considerably faster than those in the younger group
	• No sign. Differences in the females between younger and older groups
	• Thus, there was an interaction effect between age and sex for velocity
- SR significantly differed between sexes and between race distance, but not between age groups

- Sub-elite swimmers showed a mean SR of 9.5% slower, mean SL of 7.8% shorter, and a mean SI of 22.6 slower than Olympic-level swimmers

- Significant decrease in velocity for each successive race quarter in both age groups and sexes for the 100m, but no significant change in the last half of the 200m

- SI sig. decreased between successive quarters (except the 1st & 2nd quarter of the 100m)
- From 1st to last quarter, SI decreased by 20.5 and 17.9% for younger and older groups
	• SI decreased by 18.8 and 19.5% for females and males
	• SI decreased by 15.0 and 19.8% for the 100m and 200m

- SL sig decreased between the 2nd and 4th quarter for both age groups, sexes, and race distances.
- SL sig increased between the 1st and 2nd quarter in the older group and in 100m
- On avg, SL shortened from the 1st to final quarter by 4.5 and 1.6% in younger and older groups; 2.7 and 3.3% for females and males; and by 3.3 and 4.0% for 100m and 200m distances

- SR significantly decreased from the 1st to 3rd quarter in all conditions
- From 3rd-4th quarters, SR generally remained constant with the exception of the younger group and 200m, where it slightly increased
- On avg, SR decreased by 12.8 and 15.5% in younger and older groups, by 14.2% in both sexes, and by 9.3 and 12.9% in the 100 and 200m distances (between 1st and 4th quarters)
rows.Conclusion:
- Sub-elite adolescent swimmers were unable to attain the same stroke metric values as the elite-level senior swimmers
- While SR was similar between age groups, SL showed larger differences, likely leading to the larger differences in velocity
rows.Notes: - I think that this was an effective way to use MANOVA
rows.Future Research: - Future research could inspect the stroke parameter changes in masters swimmers (perhaps throughout age groups?)

rows.Title: Reproducibility of Pacing Profiles in Competitive Swimmers
rows.Aims: 1. to analyze the reproducibility of pacing profiles in high-level junior swimmers during 200, 400 and 800 m simulated competitions and to calculate the smallest worthwhile change in both overall performance, and pacing pattern
rows.Population:
- 16 competitive FR swimmers (800m: 11, 400m: 13, 200m: 12) (Unknown nation)
- 7 female, 9 males
- age 16.9 /pm 2.1
rows.Data Collection:
- Trial data consisted of simulated competition (SC) and real competition (RC)
- each athlete completed 2x**Event** trials in SC
- RC data were collected from meets during 8 weeks before/after data acquisition (via swimRankings)
- 100m split times were collected for all races
- 50m split times were collected for 200m FR
rows.Methods:
- 2-way repeated measures ANOVA (factor 1: test; factor 2: section of the test) was used to test for global effects between test and retest as well as between SC (retests used for analysis) and RC
- Cohen's d was calculated
- I identify pacing pattern, velocity for each 100m section was expressed relative to the average velocity of the whole trial
rows.Independent Variable(s):
- section of test (split)
- competition (real or simulated)
rows.Results:
- Total time in test and retest were not significantly different
- Significant gender difference was observed for the normalized profiles of males and females during the 800 and 400m tests
- Athletes adopted a hast-start profile with a sig. faster first section in each trial during SC and RC
- Differences between SC and RC ranged from 2.4s (200m) to 5.8s (800m) in males; females showed a range of 1.4s (200m) to 26.7s (800m)
- Pacing profile was similar in SC and RC -> no sig different pacing pattern
- Intra-individual differences in split times between SC and RC were small in the middle of the race during 800m and 400m
- 1st section showed higher error in both distances; last section during 400m and last 2 sections of 800m showed higher error
rows.Conclusion:
- High-level junior swimmers can perform self-paced 200, 400, and 800m bouts with good reproducibility
- The assumption that pacing profiles are stable has been particularly confirmed for the first three quarters of the race; last quarter showed increased variability
- simulated trials seem to be an acceptable model to analyse pacing profiles in competitive swimming
rows.Limitations:
- Junior swimmers may have lower stability than more experienced athletes

rows.Title: Variation vs. specialization: the dose-time-effect of technical and physiological variety in the development of elite swimmers
rows.Aims:
1. Investigate the relationship between performance level and degree of specialization
2. Quantify technical (number of different swimming strokes) and physiological variety (number of different race distances) required to become an international-class swimmer (> 750 swimming points)
rows.Population:
- 4094 swimmers (2190 females, 1904 males)
- 1,522,803 races
rows.Event:
- LC & SC (but athletes were selected based on 200m LC events)
- All events
rows.Data Collection:
- Athletes were selected based on their 200m LC performances
- Data from ages 10-26 were then retrospectively collected
rows.Methods:
Correlational Analysis
- The relationship between performance level at peak performance age and number of different swimming strokes and race distances competed in during development from early junior to elite age were examined using Pearson's or Spearman's correlation (depending on distribution)

Poisson Distribution
- dose-time effect of technical and physiological variety across the development process and the probability (p) of becoming an international-class swimmer was calculated using Poisson distribution (calculated using number of strokes and race distances)
rows.Dependent Variable(s): - Performance level at peak performance age
rows.Independent Variable(s):
- Age category (10-14, 15-17, 18-20, and 21-26)
- Performance level
- Number of different strokes and race distances
rows.Results:
Correlational Analysis
- higher ranked females of all stroke specializations competed in fewer swimming strokes after 15yrs of age; Males showed that lower technical variety was most pronounced in 200FR, BR, an FL but not IM

Poisson Distribution
- Highest probability of becoming a female international-class FR swimmer when starting to compete in either three or four strokes, ideally transitioning to 3 and 2 strokes at the ages of 12 and 19
- Male FR swimmers showed a similar pattern, except the transition from 3 to 2 strokes occurs later at 13 and 21; competing in only one stroke or all 5 strokes showed low probability to become an international-class swimmer at early junior and elite age
-  BR, BA, and FL swimmers showed lower technical variety beginning with three swimming strokes during junior age
- Higher technical variety was evident in IM of both sexes beginning with 4 during early junior age and focusing on 3 swimming strokes at 17 and 19yrs of age for females and males
- At peak performance age, BR was most frequently combined with IM; BA and FL were most frequently combined with FR

- Higher ranked FL and BA female swimmers were more specialized from 15 and 18yrs; higher ranked FR and IM male swimmers showed more variety from the beginning of their career
rows.Conclusion:
- In order to increase probability of becoming an international-class swimmer, athletes should optimize rather than maximize stroke variety
- Variety increased probability during junior age and declined towards elite age
- Female swimmers appear to specialize earlier than their male counterparts

2. Poisson distribution

rows.Aims:

- Data from LEN db
- 2021 European Championships

- applied for all swimmers and performances both in the total and split times to estimate means and within- and between-swimmer variations
- Fixed main effects were event, lap, and rounds (heat type)

ANOVA
- applied to explore differences between the CV and %diff between distances

Peason's correlation
- Between performances, CV, and %diff to assess if variability in performance was related to the swimmer's level
